In [[mathematics]], a '''ribbon category''', also called a '''tortile category''', is a particular type of [[braided monoidal category]].

== Definition ==
A [[monoidal category]] <math>\mathcal C</math> is, loosely speaking, a [[category (mathematics)|category]] equipped with a notion resembling the tensor product (of vector spaces, say). That is, for any two objects <math>C_1, C_2 \in \mathcal C</math>, there is an object <math>C_1 \otimes C_2 \in \mathcal C</math>. The assignment <math>C_1, C_2 \mapsto C_1 \otimes C_2</math> is supposed to be [[functorial]] and needs to require a number of further properties such as a unit object 1 and an [[associativity isomorphism]]. Such a category is called braided if there are [[isomorphism]]s
:<math>c_{C_1, C_2}: C_1 \otimes C_2 \stackrel \cong \rightarrow C_2 \otimes C_1.</math>

A braided monoidal category is called a ribbon category if the category is left [[rigid category|rigid]] and has a family of ''twists''. The former means that for each object <math>C</math> there is another object (called the left [[duality (mathematics)|dual]]), <math>C^*</math>, with maps
:<math>1 \rightarrow C \otimes C^*, C^* \otimes C \rightarrow 1</math>
such that the compositions
:<math>C^* \cong C^* \otimes 1 \rightarrow C^* \otimes (C \otimes C^*) \cong (C^* \otimes C) \otimes C^* \rightarrow 1 \otimes C^* \cong C^*</math>
equals the identity of <math>C^*</math>, and similarly with <math>C</math>. The twists are maps 
:<math>C \in \mathcal C</math>, <math>\theta_C : C \rightarrow C</math>
such that
:<math>\begin{align}
    \theta_{C_1 \otimes C_2} &= c_{C_2, C_1} c_{C_1, C_2} (\theta_{C_1}  \otimes \theta_{C_2})\\
    \theta_1 &= \mathrm{id}\\
    \theta_{C^*} & = (\theta_C)^*.
\end{align}</math>
To be a ribbon category, the duals have to be thus compatible with the braiding and the twists.

=== Concrete Example ===
Consider the category <math>\mathbf{FdVect}(\mathbb{C})</math> of finite-dimensional vector spaces over <math>\mathbb{C}</math>. Suppose that <math>C</math> is such a vector space, spanned by the basis vectors <math>\hat{e_1}, \hat{e_2},\cdots,\hat{e_n}</math>. We assign to <math>C</math> the dual object <math>C^\dagger</math> spanned by the basis vectors <math>\hat{e}^1, \hat{e}^2,\cdots,\hat{e}^n</math>. Then let us define

:<math>\begin{align}
    \cdot: \ C^\dagger\otimes C &\to 1\\
    \hat{e}^i\cdot\hat{e_j} &\mapsto \begin{cases} 1 & i=j \\ 0 & i\neq j \end{cases}
\end{align}</math>

and its dual

:<math>\begin{align}
    k I_n:  1& \to C\otimes C^\dagger\\
    k &\mapsto k \sum_{i=1}^n \hat{e_i}\otimes \hat{e}^i\\
      &= \begin{pmatrix}k & 0 & \cdots & 0\\ 0 & k & &\vdots \\ &&\ddots&\\0&\cdots &&k\end{pmatrix}
\end{align}</math>

(which largely amounts to assigning a given <math>\hat{e_i}</math> the dual <math>\hat{e}^i</math>).

Then indeed we find that (for example) 

:<math>\begin{align}
    \hat{e}^i &\cong \hat{e}^i\otimes 1 \\
    &\underset{I_n}{\to} \hat{e}^i \otimes \sum_{j=1}^n \hat{e_j}\otimes \hat{e}^j\\
    &\cong \sum_{j=1}^n \left(\hat{e}^i \otimes \hat{e_j}\right)\otimes \hat{e}^j\\
    &\underset{\cdot}{\to} \sum_{j=1}^n \begin{cases} 1 \otimes \hat{e}^j & i=j \\ 0 \otimes \hat{e}^j & i\neq j \end{cases}\\
    &= 1\otimes \hat{e}^i \cong \hat{e}^i
\end{align}</math>

and similarly for <math>\hat{e_i}</math>. Since this proof applies to any [[Dimension (vector space)|finite-dimensional vector space]], we have shown that our structure over <math>\mathbf{FdVect}</math> defines a (left) rigid monoidal category. 

Then, we must define braids and twists in such a way that they are compatible. In this case, this largely makes one determined given the other on the reals. For example, if we take the trivial braiding

:<math>\begin{align}
c_{C_1,C_2}: C_1 \otimes C_2 &\to C_2 \otimes C_1\\
             c_{C_1, C_2} (a, b) &\mapsto (b, a)
\end{align}</math>

then <math>c_{C_1, C_2} c_{C_2, C_1}=\mathrm{id}_{C_1\otimes C_2}</math>, so our twist must obey <math>\theta_{C_1 \otimes C_2} = \theta_{C_1} \otimes \theta_{C_2}</math>. In other words it must operate elementwise across tensor products. But any object <math>C\in\mathbf{FdVect}</math> can be written in the form <math>C=\bigotimes_{i=1}^n 1</math> for some <math>n</math>, <math>\theta_C=\bigotimes_{i=1}^n \theta_1 = \bigotimes_{i=1}^n \mathrm{id} = \mathrm{id}_C</math>, so our twists must also be trivial. 

On the other hand, we can introduce any nonzero multiplicative factor into the above braiding rule without breaking isomorphism (at least in <math>\mathbb{C}</math>). Let us for example take the braiding

:<math>\begin{align}
c_{C_1,C_2}: C_1 \otimes C_2 &\to C_2 \otimes C_1\\
            c_{C_1, C_2} (a, b) &\mapsto i (b, a)
\end{align}</math>

Then <math>c_{C_1, C_2} c_{C_2, C_1}=-\mathrm{id}_{C_1\otimes C_2}</math>. Since <math>\theta_1 = \mathrm{id}</math>, then <math>\theta_{1 \otimes 1} = -\mathrm{id}_{1\otimes 1}</math>; by induction, if <math>C</math> is <math>n</math>-dimensional, then <math>\theta_C = (-1)^{n+1} \mathrm{id}_C</math>.

=== Other Examples ===

* The category of [[projective module]]s over a [[commutative ring]]. In this category, the monoidal structure is the [[tensor product]], the dual object is the [[dual (linear algebra)|dual]] in the sense of (linear) algebra, which is again projective. The twists in this case are the [[identity map]]s. 
* A more sophisticated example of a ribbon category are finite-dimensional representations of a [[quantum group]].<ref>{{harvnb|Turaev|2020|loc=XI. An algebraic construction of modular categories}}</ref>

The name ribbon category is motivated by a graphical depiction of morphisms.<ref>{{harvnb|Turaev|2020|p=25}}</ref>

== Variant ==

A '''strongly ribbon category''' is a ribbon category '''''C''''' equipped with a [[dagger category|dagger structure]] such that the [[functor]] †: '''''C'''''<sup>[[opposite category|op]]</sup> → '''''C''''' coherently preserves the ribbon structure.
